title: Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa
summary: In the span of a few hours on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would be implementing a fee of over $103,000 on H-1B visas, and news broke that the State Department plans on revoking the visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers - which, according to The…
whatHappening: The Trump administration is sharply raising barriers for foreign workers and asylum seekers. The Department of Homeland Security announced a fee exceeding $103,000 on H-1B visas, while the State Department simultaneously moved to revoke visas for up to 200,000 asylum seekers.
whoInvolved: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), a federal executive department responsible for immigration, customs, and border control, is implementing the H-1B fee increase. The State Department is handling the asylum visa revocations. Big Tech companies, which rely heavily on H-1B visas to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations, are the intended targets of the policy.
whyMatters: The H-1B fee hike could substantially increase costs for technology companies that depend on foreign talent for software engineering and other specialized roles. The simultaneous asylum visa revocations represent a dramatic tightening of U.S. immigration policy that could affect hundreds of thousands of people seeking refuge. Together, these moves signal a major shift in how the administration approaches both skilled migration and humanitarian protection.
articleBody:
The Trump administration is simultaneously tightening immigration pathways on two fronts. On Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced plans to implement a fee exceeding $103,000 on H-1B visas, the visa classification that allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations. Hours later, news broke that the State Department intends to revoke the visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers, according to The Verge.

The H-1B visa program has long been central to how technology companies staff their engineering and technical teams. Under current regulations, the USCIS, an agency within the Department of Homeland Security, manages the H-1B classification alongside other visa programs. The proposed fee of over $103,000 per visa would represent a dramatic increase in the cost of hiring foreign workers through this channel, effectively pricing many companies out of the program or forcing them to absorb substantially higher labor expenses.

The timing and scope of both announcements underscore a comprehensive reshaping of U.S. immigration policy. The visa revocations targeting asylum seekers represent a separate but parallel effort to restrict entry, affecting a much larger population than the H-1B changes. The asylum visa program serves individuals fleeing persecution, and revoking up to 200,000 visas would represent an extraordinary reduction in humanitarian immigration.

Tech industry reliance on H-1B workers is well documented, with companies citing talent shortages in specialized fields as justification for the program. A fee exceeding $100,000 would fundamentally alter the economics of hiring foreign workers, likely pushing some companies to either hire domestically, shift operations abroad, or reduce headcount. For startups and mid-size firms with tighter budgets, the fee could be prohibitively expensive.

The dual policy announcements reflect a significant ideological shift in how the administration views immigration across the spectrum. Rather than distinguishing between different categories of immigration—skilled workers, asylum seekers, or other groups—the policy approach treats immigration broadly as something to be restricted and made more expensive. The scale of the asylum visa revocations, affecting up to 200,000 people, suggests this approach extends well beyond the technology sector.

title: At just $8, you owe it to yourself to grab Inscryption
summary: What starts as a roguelite deckbuilder builds into something far more ambitious. | Image: Daniel Mullins Games/Devolver Digital If you watched the Gamescom 2026 announcements, you might have caught a trailer for the bizarre, frenetic Pony Island 2: Panda Circus, a game from…
whatHappening: The Verge is highlighting Inscryption, the 2021 roguelike deck-building game, as an exceptional value at just $8. The article suggests the game delivers far more ambitious gameplay than its roguelite deckbuilder premise initially suggests.
whoInvolved: Inscryption was developed by Daniel Mullins Games and published by Devolver Digital, with director Daniel Mullins leading the project. The game has since expanded across multiple platforms including Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch, and Xbox.
whyMatters: At a price point of $8, Inscryption represents strong value for players seeking substantial gaming experiences. The game's critical recognition and multi-platform availability have made it accessible to a broad audience, demonstrating the commercial viability of indie titles that blend multiple genres.
articleBody:
Inscryption, the 2021 roguelike deck-building game from Daniel Mullins Games and published by Devolver Digital, is drawing renewed attention for its exceptional value proposition. According to The Verge, at just $8, the game warrants serious consideration from both casual and dedicated gamers seeking meaningful gameplay experiences.

What distinguishes Inscryption from standard roguelite offerings is its scope and ambition. The game begins as a traditional deckbuilder, with players constructing and refining card decks to battle opponents. However, the experience evolves significantly beyond this initial framework, incorporating elements that expand the game's narrative and mechanical complexity in unexpected ways.

Since its October 19, 2021 release on Windows, Inscryption has been ported extensively across the gaming landscape. The title is now available on Linux, macOS, PlayStation 4 and 5, Nintendo Switch, and Xbox One and Series X/S platforms. This broad distribution has made the game accessible to players regardless of their preferred hardware, contributing to its reach within the gaming community.

The premise places players in a cabin where a mysterious gamemaster compels them to engage in a tabletop card game, establishing an atmospheric framework that drives the gameplay experience. This setup creates tension and intrigue that carries forward throughout the player's progression, distinguishing the title from more straightforward deckbuilders.

At an $8 price point, Inscryption represents compelling value in an industry where many indie titles command $20 or more. The combination of accessible pricing, proven critical acclaim, and substantial gameplay content makes it an attractive proposition for players looking to expand their gaming library without significant financial commitment. The game's success across multiple platforms suggests that creative, ambitious indie experiences continue to resonate with audiences when priced appropriately.

title: Garmin’s new Fenix 9 adds brighter screens and smoother map panning
summary: The Garmin Fenix 9. | Image: Garmin Garmin just took the wraps off its new line of rugged Fenix 9 smartwatches, with the base model featuring an OLED display with a brightness of up to 3,000 nits, making it twice as bright as its predecessor. Starting at $999.99 for the 43mm…
whatHappening: Garmin has unveiled its new Fenix 9 line of rugged smartwatches, featuring significantly brighter OLED displays and improved map navigation. The base 43mm model starts at $999.99 and boasts a display brightness of up to 3,000 nits—double that of its predecessor.
whoInvolved: Garmin Ltd., an American multinational technology company headquartered in Olathe, Kansas, is behind the release. The company specializes in GPS-enabled products and navigation devices across automotive, aviation, marine, outdoors, and sports markets.
whyMatters: The substantial increase in display brightness addresses a key pain point for outdoor smartwatch users, making the device far more usable in direct sunlight and challenging conditions. Smoother map panning enhances the user experience for outdoor enthusiasts, potentially solidifying Garmin's position in the premium rugged smartwatch segment as consumer demand for high-performance wearables continues to grow.
articleBody:
Garmin has officially introduced its latest flagship smartwatch line, the Fenix 9, marking a significant upgrade to the popular rugged wearable series. According to The Verge, the base 43mm model features an OLED display with brightness reaching up to 3,000 nits—a substantial leap from the previous generation, which maxed out at 1,500 nits. This doubling of brightness represents one of the most notable improvements in the new lineup.

The Fenix 9 addresses a common frustration among outdoor smartwatch users: visibility in bright conditions. The enhanced display brightness makes the watch far more legible under direct sunlight, a critical feature for hikers, runners, and adventurers who rely on their devices in open environments. Beyond the brighter screen, Garmin has also refined the map panning functionality, offering smoother navigation through digital maps—a feature that benefits users planning routes or exploring unfamiliar terrain.

Garmin Ltd., based in Olathe, Kansas, has built its reputation as a leader in GPS-enabled navigation products and sensor-based devices across multiple markets including automotive, aviation, marine, outdoors, and sports. The Fenix line has long been the company's premium offering for serious outdoor enthusiasts, combining durability with sophisticated navigation and fitness tracking capabilities.

The Fenix 9's starting price of $999.99 positions it at the premium end of the smartwatch market, reflecting the advanced technology and rugged construction buyers can expect. The investment in OLED technology and brightness enhancements suggests Garmin is responding directly to user feedback about display performance in outdoor conditions.

The release of the Fenix 9 underscores Garmin's continued focus on the outdoor and sports segments of the wearable market. As consumers increasingly seek high-performance devices that can handle extreme conditions and demanding activities, innovations in display technology and navigation responsiveness become key differentiators. The brighter screen and smoother map interaction represent tangible improvements that directly enhance the user experience for the adventurers and athletes who depend on these tools.

title: Apple’s ‘new’ polishing cloth is the same except $10 cheaper
summary: Apple just dropped a new polishing cloth, and unlike its refreshed Mac Mini models, it comes with a price cut, as spotted earlier by MacRumors. The polishing cloth is still "made with soft, nonabrasive material" but costs $9 instead of $19. It doesn't look like anything else has…
whatHappening: Apple has released a new polishing cloth priced at $9, down from the original $19 version. The product maintains the same soft, nonabrasive material specifications but undercuts its predecessor by 50 percent.
whoInvolved: Apple Inc., the American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California, is releasing the discounted cloth. MacRumors, a website that aggregates Apple-related news and rumors, first spotted the price reduction.
whyMatters: The price cut signals a potential shift in Apple's premium pricing strategy for accessories, suggesting the company may be recalibrating its polishing cloth as a value item rather than a luxury accessory. This move comes as Apple continues refreshing its product lineup, including new Mac Mini models, offering consumers cost savings on complementary products.
articleBody:
Apple has quietly introduced a new version of its polishing cloth at a significantly reduced price point. The cloth, which now costs $9, represents a 50 percent discount from the original $19 price tag that accompanied Apple's initial launch of the premium accessory. According to MacRumors, the specifications remain largely unchanged—the cloth is still manufactured from soft, nonabrasive material designed for cleaning Apple's displays and other sensitive surfaces.

The timing of this release is noteworthy given Apple's broader product refresh cycle. The company has just unveiled refreshed Mac Mini models alongside the polishing cloth release, yet unlike those computers, the cloth arrives with consumer-friendly pricing rather than premium positioning. This contrasts with Apple's typical approach to accessories, which have often commanded high prices relative to functionally similar third-party alternatives.

Apple Inc., founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, has built its reputation on premium consumer electronics and carefully curated product ecosystems. The company's current focus spans consumer electronics, software, and online services following its expansion beyond computers beginning in 2007. Historically, Apple's accessories have reflected this premium positioning, with products priced to reinforce the brand's luxury market perception.

The polishing cloth itself emerged as an unlikely focal point of discussion when Apple first introduced it alongside the high-end Studio Display and other premium products. At $19, the accessory became a subject of industry commentary, with observers noting the price seemed steep for a simple cleaning cloth. The new $9 version suggests Apple may have reconsidered this positioning, opting instead to make the product more accessible to a broader audience.

Whether this price adjustment indicates a permanent shift in Apple's accessory strategy remains unclear. The reduction could reflect customer feedback, competitive pressure, or simply a decision to position the cloth as an entry-level accessory rather than a premium product. Regardless, the move offers existing and prospective customers a more economical way to maintain their Apple devices with manufacturer-approved materials.

title: Lenovo confirms Legion Go issues after gamers report bricked devices
summary: Cursed BIOS. | Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge When a company's software update turns your computer into a useless brick, should fixes be free? Framework, the modular computer startup, apparently thinks so. But it's not clear that computing giant Lenovo will go that far.…
whatHappening: Lenovo's Legion Go gaming device has reportedly been bricked by a faulty BIOS software update, leaving some users with non-functional hardware. The company now faces questions about whether it will provide free repairs or replacements for affected customers.
whoInvolved: Lenovo Group Limited is a Hong Kong-based Chinese multinational technology corporation headquartered in Beijing and Morrisville, North Carolina, specializing in personal computers and consumer electronics. Framework Computer, an American PC manufacturer known for championing the right-to-repair movement, has already committed to free fixes for similar update failures on its own devices.
whyMatters: The incident highlights the growing risk that software updates pose to consumer hardware and raises expectations around manufacturer accountability when defects render devices unusable. Lenovo's response—or lack thereof—will signal to consumers and competitors alike whether major tech companies will bear the cost of their own software failures or pass the burden to customers.
articleBody:
Lenovo has acknowledged problems with its Legion Go handheld gaming device after multiple gamers reported their units becoming completely non-functional following a BIOS software update. According to The Verge, the issue centers on what users have described as a "cursed BIOS," rendering devices inoperable and leaving owners uncertain whether they can recover their hardware.

The timing of the issue draws a stark contrast with how competitors handle similar failures. Framework Computer, the American startup that designs easily repairable modular laptops, has already announced it will provide free fixes to customers whose devices were affected by problematic software updates. The company's commitment reflects its broader philosophy as a proponent of the right-to-repair movement, positioning itself around user empowerment and product longevity.

Lenovo Group Limited, by contrast, has not yet committed to a clear remediation path. As a multinational corporation specializing in personal computers and consumer electronics with global operations spanning research centers in Beijing and North Carolina, Lenovo commands substantial resources. However, the company has historically approached warranty and repair policies differently than smaller, repair-focused competitors.

The distinction matters because it sets precedent for how the industry treats software-induced hardware failures. When a manufacturer's own update renders a device unusable, consumer expectations—and possibly legal interpretations of warranty obligations—increasingly point toward manufacturer responsibility. Framework's decision to absorb costs positions free repairs as a competitive advantage and a signal of confidence in its products.

Gamers affected by the Legion Go issue now face uncertainty about their options. Some may be eligible for warranty coverage, while others could face out-of-pocket repair costs depending on Lenovo's final policy decision. The company's response will likely influence consumer trust in future Legion Go purchases and in Lenovo's broader gaming brand.

title: Zillow and Redfin settle FTC antitrust case over their rental listings partnership
summary: The FTC and Zillow have announced a settlement that ends the case alleging that a 2025 "partnership" between Zillow and Redfin violated antitrust laws. The FTC had alleged Zillow agreed to pay Redfin to syndicate its listings, while Redfin would end its own advertising contracts…
whatHappening: The FTC and Zillow have reached a settlement ending an antitrust case that challenged a 2025 partnership between Zillow and Redfin. The deal allegedly involved Zillow paying Redfin to syndicate listings while Redfin would discontinue its own advertising contracts—a structure the FTC argued violated antitrust law.
whoInvolved: Zillow Group, Inc., a real-estate marketplace company founded in 2006 by former Microsoft executives including Rich Barton and Lloyd Frink, and Redfin, a real estate services subsidiary of Rocket Companies that operates in the U.S. and Canada. The Federal Trade Commission brought the case alleging anticompetitive conduct.
whyMatters: The settlement clarifies limits on how competing real-estate platforms can structure deals involving listing syndication and advertising exclusivity. The outcome will influence future partnerships in the fragmented real-estate digital marketplace and may reshape how platforms balance competitive reach with partnership arrangements.
articleBody:
The Federal Trade Commission has reached a settlement with Zillow in a case alleging that a proposed partnership between Zillow and Redfin would have violated antitrust laws. According to The Verge, the FTC had challenged the arrangement on grounds that it would have reduced competition in the rental listings market through an agreement in which Zillow would pay Redfin to syndicate its listings in exchange for Redfin ending its own advertising contracts.

Zillow Group, Inc., founded in 2006 by former Microsoft executives Rich Barton and Lloyd Frink—who previously founded the travel platform Expedia—operates one of the largest real-estate marketplaces in the United States. Redfin, a subsidiary of Rocket Companies, provides real estate agent services for buying, selling, and renting homes across the U.S. and Canada. The two companies had announced their partnership for 2025, which would have created a significant realignment in how listings are distributed and promoted across competing platforms.

The FTC's challenge focused on the structure of the deal: by paying Redfin to syndicate listings rather than allowing Redfin to independently decide whether to advertise competing inventory, the arrangement would have reduced Redfin's incentive to compete for advertising placements. This, the FTC argued, would ultimately harm consumers by limiting competitive choices in how rental properties are advertised and discovered online.

The settlement resolves the case without determining whether the partnership would have actually violated antitrust law, and the terms of the settlement remain subject to the specifics outlined in the agreement. Such settlements typically require companies to unwind the challenged arrangement or to agree to modified terms that address the FTC's competitive concerns.

The case reflects ongoing regulatory scrutiny of major technology platforms in the real-estate sector, where listing syndication and advertising placement have become critical competitive battlegrounds. As Zillow and Redfin both operate major platforms with significant market presence, decisions about how they distribute and promote listings ripple across the entire industry, affecting smaller brokers, agents, and ultimately consumers searching for homes.

title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
summary: The creator of the world's first 3D-printed gun claims he's developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms. It's an opening volley in what's shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of…
whatHappening: The creator of the first 3D-printed gun claims to have developed a method to bypass government-mandated software designed to prevent 3D printers from manufacturing firearms. This move opens a new front in an escalating regulatory battle between law enforcement and those pushing to democratize gun manufacturing through digital design.
whoInvolved: Cody Wilson, founder of Defense Distributed, is at the center of this dispute. Wilson is a gun rights activist and crypto-anarchist whose organization publishes open-source firearm designs as CAD files for 3D printing and CNC milling. Defense Distributed gained international attention in 2013 when it released plans for the Liberator, the first widely available functioning 3D-printed pistol.
whyMatters: This escalation threatens to undermine regulatory efforts to control homemade firearm production and distribution. If Wilson's workaround proves viable and spreads, it could render software-based restrictions ineffective, forcing regulators into a perpetual cycle of technological cat-and-mouse with no clear endpoint. The outcome will likely shape how governments approach digital manufacturing oversight for years to come.
articleBody:
The battle over 3D-printed firearms is entering a new phase. According to The Verge, the creator of the world's first 3D-printed gun now claims to have developed a method to circumvent government-mandated software designed to block 3D printers from producing firearms. This move represents an opening salvo in what appears to be an escalating conflict between regulatory authorities seeking to stem the proliferation of homemade weapons and advocates pushing to democratize firearm manufacturing through digital design.

Cody Wilson, the founder of Defense Distributed, has been at the forefront of this movement since 2013, when his organization published plans for the Liberator—the first widely available functioning 3D-printed pistol. Defense Distributed operates as an open-source hardware and software organization, developing digital schematics for firearms as CAD files available for download and use in 3D printing or CNC milling applications. Wilson, a gun rights activist and crypto-anarchist, has framed the work as supporting the popular production of homemade firearms, positioning it as a matter of democratic access to manufacturing capability.

Governments around the world have moved to restrict access to these designs and manufacturing capabilities. In response to the proliferation of 3D-printed gun plans, regulators have pursued software-based solutions intended to prevent 3D printers from executing files containing firearm components. These mandates represent a technological approach to a novel problem: how to control what can be manufactured when the tools themselves are becoming more widely available and harder to regulate.

Wilson's claimed breakthrough in circumventing this software represents a fundamental challenge to that regulatory strategy. If his method proves effective and becomes widely known, it could render software locks largely obsolete, forcing governments back to the drawing board. The implications extend beyond firearms themselves—the underlying conflict reflects broader tensions over digital manufacturing, open-source design, and the extent to which governments can control what gets made in an era of increasingly accessible production technology.

The stakes are particularly high because this is not a static battle but an evolving one. Each regulatory innovation will likely be met with countermeasures, creating a dynamic cycle in which neither side can claim permanent victory. Unlike traditional gun regulation, which relies on supply chains and physical manufacturing infrastructure, digital firearm design operates at the speed of software development and information distribution.

title: Raspberry Pi shares its official tutorial for making a cyberdeck
summary: Raspberry Pi's head of social, Ashley Whittaker, acknowledged the cyberdeck trend today, saying "we haven't been able to get away from cyberdecks this year." Tiny portable computers made out of things like purses, jewelry boxes, and other thrifted or recycled parts have gone…
whatHappening: Raspberry Pi has officially embraced the cyberdeck trend by releasing a tutorial for building one, acknowledging that these custom portable computers have become impossible to ignore in the maker community. The company's head of social media noted that cyberdecks have dominated conversations around the platform throughout the year.
whoInvolved: Raspberry Pi, a UK-based manufacturer of small single-board computers (SBCs) originally developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation in collaboration with Broadcom, is taking an official stance on the cyberdeck movement. Ashley Whittaker, Raspberry Pi's head of social, is the company representative quoted on the trend.
whyMatters: By releasing an official cyberdeck tutorial, Raspberry Pi is legitimizing a grassroots maker movement while capitalizing on growing demand for customizable portable computing devices. This move signals that niche hardware trends can transition into mainstream recognition when they reach critical mass in the enthusiast community.
articleBody:
Raspberry Pi, the UK-based manufacturer of single-board computers, has officially weighed in on one of this year's biggest maker trends: cyberdecks. According to The Verge, Ashley Whittaker, Raspberry Pi's head of social, acknowledged the cyberdeck phenomenon by saying the company "hasn't been able to get away from cyberdecks this year."

A cyberdeck is a custom-built, portable personal computer typically designed for individualized purposes and featuring a cyberpunk aesthetic. These devices are individually crafted by makers using laptop motherboards or single-board computers like Raspberry Pis, and they incorporate displays, keyboards, and housings made from thrifted or recycled materials such as purses, jewelry boxes, and other repurposed objects. The aesthetic appeals to a growing community of DIY computer enthusiasts who view computing hardware as a canvas for creative expression.

Raspberry Pi's decision to publish an official tutorial represents a significant shift in how the company engages with grassroots maker culture. By providing guidance on cyberdeck construction, the company is not simply acknowledging the trend—it is actively participating in and legitimizing it. This move transforms cyberdecks from an underground niche hobby into something with corporate backing and institutional support.

The timing reflects the rapid acceleration of the cyberdeck movement within the maker community. What began as scattered individual projects by hobbyists has evolved into a recognizable subculture with its own aesthetics, communities, and shared design principles. Raspberry Pi's involvement suggests the trend has reached a tipping point where ignoring it was no longer feasible for a company whose products are at the core of many of these builds.

For Raspberry Pi Holdings, the company's commercial entity, this tutorial represents both a marketing opportunity and a genuine engagement with its user base. Single-board computers have always been positioned as educational and hackable devices, and cyberdecks embody exactly that spirit—transforming commodity hardware into something personalized and unique. By providing official guidance, Raspberry Pi strengthens its brand identity as a platform for creative makers rather than just a component supplier.

title: We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is an intimate coming-of-age horror film
summary: Jane Schoenbrun's latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, is making a splash in theaters right now. So it seems like the perfect time to revisit their first film, We're All Going to the World's Fair. I fell in love with this film when I first saw it at Sundance in…
whatHappening: Jane Schoenbrun's debut film We're All Going to the World's Fair is getting renewed attention as the filmmaker's latest project, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, gains traction in theaters. The Verge is revisiting Schoenbrun's intimate coming-of-age horror film, which premiered at Sundance.
whoInvolved: Jane Schoenbrun is an American filmmaker known for directing We're All Going to the World's Fair (2021), I Saw the TV Glow (2024), and Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (2026). The Verge, a technology and culture publication, is covering the story.
whyMatters: Schoenbrun's emergence as a distinctive voice in independent horror cinema is significant for the future of the genre, particularly in how filmmakers approach coming-of-age narratives through a horror lens. The continued critical interest in their work signals growing audience appetite for unconventional, intimate takes on the genre.
articleBody:
Jane Schoenbrun's debut feature We're All Going to the World's Fair continues to resonate with audiences and critics years after its initial release, even as the filmmaker's career has accelerated with new projects entering theaters. According to The Verge, the timing of Schoenbrun's latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, offers an opportune moment to revisit the intimate coming-of-age horror film that introduced many viewers to their distinctive directorial vision.

We're All Going to the World's Fair premiered at the Sundance Film Festival, the largest independent film festival in the United States, where it made an immediate impression. The film's blend of horror and coming-of-age storytelling struck a particular chord with critics and audiences, with The Verge's coverage noting the author's personal connection to the work from its festival debut.

Schoenbrun has built a remarkably prolific career in the years since We're All Going to the World's Fair's release. Following their debut, they directed I Saw the TV Glow in 2024, and their work has continued to evolve and attract attention as each new project arrives. The rapid succession of films from Schoenbrun suggests a filmmaker working at peak creative capacity, pushing the boundaries of what horror and coming-of-age narratives can explore.

The decision to revisit We're All Going to the World's Fair in light of Schoenbrun's newer work reflects the film's lasting impact on independent cinema. What made the debut so compelling—its intimacy, its willingness to find horror in the texture of adolescent experience—remains relevant even as the filmmaker's subsequent projects expand and refine those initial artistic impulses.

For viewers encountering Schoenbrun's work for the first time through their recent releases, returning to We're All Going to the World's Fair offers insight into the artistic foundations of a filmmaker whose voice has only grown more confident and distinctive.

title: Two great new repairable gadgets
summary: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 141, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you're new here, welcome, I'm newish here too, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.) This week, I've been getting back into the Installer…
whatHappening: The Verge's Installer newsletter has highlighted two new gadgets that prioritize repairability, a growing consumer concern. The featured products represent a shift toward devices designed to be fixed rather than replaced.
whoInvolved: The Verge, a technology and culture publication, curates consumer gadget recommendations through its Installer newsletter series. The newsletter, now in its 141st edition, serves as a guide to notable technology products and consumer goods.
whyMatters: The spotlight on repairable gadgets reflects increasing consumer demand for sustainable technology and reduced electronic waste. As manufacturers face pressure to extend product lifecycles, repairability has become a competitive differentiator in the consumer electronics market, affecting both environmental impact and long-term ownership costs.
articleBody:
Consumer electronics have long followed a pattern of planned obsolescence, with manufacturers designing products meant to be discarded rather than repaired. But a new wave of gadgets is challenging that approach by prioritizing durability and user-friendly fixes. According to The Verge, this week's Installer newsletter features two standout products that exemplify this shift toward repairability.

The move toward repairable gadgets addresses a mounting problem: electronic waste. When devices cannot be easily serviced or upgraded, consumers face the choice of either living with degraded performance or purchasing replacements entirely. This cycle has contributed to millions of tons of e-waste annually, filled with valuable materials and toxic components. By designing products that users can repair themselves or service through accessible channels, manufacturers can significantly extend the useful life of their goods.

The Installer series has built its reputation on identifying products that matter to consumers seeking quality and thoughtful design. The newsletter's 141st edition continues this tradition while reflecting broader market changes. Tech companies increasingly recognize that repairability appeals to environmentally conscious consumers and can reduce support costs through customer self-service repairs. Right-to-repair movements have also pressured manufacturers to make spare parts and repair documentation more accessible.

These two featured gadgets represent different product categories, yet share a common philosophy: devices should be serviceable throughout their lifespan. Whether through modular designs that allow component swaps, easily replaceable batteries, or straightforward access to internal parts, repairable products reduce the barrier between a malfunctioning device and a working one. This approach benefits consumers economically while supporting sustainability goals.

As consumer awareness of e-waste and product lifecycles grows, repairability is becoming a key purchasing criterion alongside traditional factors like performance and price. The gadgets highlighted in this week's Installer stand as evidence that the market is responding to these shifting priorities, with manufacturers investing in designs that prove devices can be both innovative and lasting.

title: GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series
summary: It’s been over a decade and two console generations since GTA V came out, and its sequel is still a work in progress. GTA VI has faced multiple delays, with developer Rockstar Games bumping back its predicted release date twice, first to May 26th, 2026, then again to November…
whatHappening: Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited sequel to Rockstar Games' flagship franchise, has been delayed again—this time to November 2026. The game, which has faced multiple pushbacks over more than a decade of development, remains a work in progress at the studio.
whoInvolved: Rockstar Games, the American video game publisher based in New York City and a subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive, is developing GTA VI through its British development house Rockstar North. The studio is led by president Sam Houser, one of the founding brothers who has overseen the Grand Theft Auto series since its creation.
whyMatters: GTA VI is one of the most anticipated releases in gaming, and the repeated delays signal ongoing challenges in developing a sequel to one of the best-selling franchises in entertainment history. The extended timeline affects not only gamers awaiting the game, but also Rockstar Games' parent company Take-Two Interactive and the broader industry's release schedule.
articleBody:
Rockstar Games has pushed back the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI once again, with the publisher now targeting November 2026 as the new release date. According to The Verge, the game has faced multiple delays, with developer Rockstar Games initially bumping back its predicted release to May 26th, 2026, before delaying it further to the fall. The extended development timeline underscores the complexity of creating a new mainline entry in one of gaming's most successful franchises.

More than a decade has passed since Grand Theft Auto V's release, and two full console generations have come and gone. The original GTA V launched in 2013 and went on to become a cultural phenomenon, generating billions in revenue and remaining commercially viable through online updates and re-releases. That longevity has set an extraordinarily high bar for its successor, placing significant pressure on Rockstar to deliver a game that justifies the wait.

Rockstar Games, established in December 1998 as a subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive, has built its reputation on sprawling open-world games that push technical and creative boundaries. The company was founded by industry veterans including brothers Dan and Sam Houser, who later oversaw development of the Grand Theft Auto series. The franchise itself, created by David Jones and Mike Dailly, has been developed under the oversight of the Houser brothers alongside Leslie Benzies and Aaron Garbut, with Rockstar North handling primary development duties.

The repeated delays reflect the scale of ambition behind GTA VI. Creating a new mainline Grand Theft Auto game requires not only advanced technical work across multiple platforms, but also the design and implementation of sprawling virtual worlds filled with detailed missions, characters, and systems. The gap since GTA V's release means players and industry observers have built substantial expectations, raising the stakes for a release that must justify over a decade of anticipation.

With November 2026 now targeted, Rockstar Games and its parent company Take-Two Interactive have signaled their commitment to releasing a finished product rather than rushing the game to market. The decision reflects a calculated approach: missing another deadline would be far more damaging than the delays themselves have proven to be.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI exists in its own universe
summary: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on GTA VI and the state of the video game industry, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers' inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it…
whatHappening: Grand Theft Auto VI is being developed as a self-contained universe distinct from previous entries in the franchise. The upcoming game, set in the fictional state of Leonida and featuring the criminal duo Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, marks a deliberate creative shift for Rockstar Games.
whoInvolved: Rockstar Games, the New York City-based video game publisher and subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive, is developing the title. The studio, headed by president Sam Houser, has been a dominant force in open-world game design since its 1998 founding.
whyMatters: This universe-building approach suggests Rockstar is rethinking how it connects or separates its flagship franchise entries, potentially influencing how players experience the game's narrative and world. The decision reflects broader industry trends toward standalone storytelling within established franchises and could shape expectations for how GTA VI relates to its predecessor, 2013's Grand Theft Auto V.
articleBody:
Rockstar Games is crafting Grand Theft Auto VI as its own distinct universe, a creative decision that underscores the studio's approach to the eighth main entry in its iconic franchise. The game, set within the fictional US state of Leonida—a Florida-inspired setting—centers on the story of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a romantic criminal duo navigating an open world that includes the Miami-inspired Vice City. According to The Verge, this universe-building framework represents a notable departure in how Rockstar is positioning the game within the broader Grand Theft Auto canon.

The decision to establish GTA VI in its own universe comes as Rockstar Games prepares for one of the most anticipated releases in the video game industry. As the sixteenth entry overall in the franchise, GTA VI follows a thirteen-year gap since Grand Theft Auto V's 2013 debut. That predecessor became a cultural phenomenon and one of the best-selling games of all time, setting an extraordinarily high bar for its successor. By anchoring GTA VI in a self-contained narrative world, Rockstar appears to be signaling that players should approach this entry on its own terms rather than as a direct continuation of the previous game's storyline and setting.

This creative choice has implications for how the game will be received and experienced by both longtime fans and newcomers. A dedicated universe allows Rockstar to establish fresh storytelling without being constrained by the narrative baggage of Grand Theft Auto V, while still maintaining the core gameplay mechanics and open-world design that define the franchise. The focus on the romantic criminal narrative of Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval suggests the studio is exploring character-driven storytelling as a central pillar of the experience.

For Rockstar Games, headed by president Sam Houser since the studio's 1998 founding, the approach reflects a matured understanding of franchise management in an era where players increasingly expect meaningful narrative depth from AAA experiences. The company's deliberate framing of GTA VI as its own universe may also serve a practical purpose: it allows the studio to innovate on the formula without having to reconcile continuity with earlier games or address why certain characters or locations may have changed.

As development continues, the universe-building framework will likely influence discussions around GTA VI's place in gaming history and whether it can match the unprecedented commercial and cultural success of its predecessor.

whoInvolved: W. He has also hosted FXX's Totally Biased with W. Kamau Bell and co-hosts multiple podcasts including Politically Re-Active.
whyMatters: Bell's perspective on indispensable tools offers insight into how a multimedia creator and social commentator—someone who works across stand-up, television, and podcasting—prioritizes his work. His selection may resonate with audiences navigating similar questions about what truly matters in their own professional and creative lives.
articleBody:
W. Kamau Bell has weighed in on a deceptively simple question: what is the most practical and indispensable tool one could possess? According to The Verge, the answer Bell offers is surprisingly straightforward, though the coverage itself seems to revel in the mystery of his choice.

Bell, whose career has spanned multiple media formats, brings a well-honed perspective to such questions. Since launching his stand-up career, he has built a reputation as a sharp cultural observer who blends comedy with substantive social commentary. His television work—including the Emmy-winning United Shades of America, which documented his travels across diverse American communities from 2016 to 2022—demonstrates someone accustomed to working with whatever tools enable him to connect with and understand his subjects.

Throughout his career in broadcast media and podcasting, Bell has consistently adapted to different platforms and formats. His run hosting FXX's Totally Biased with W. Kamau Bell from 2012 to 2013 required managing production requirements; his current work on the live radio show and podcast Kamau Right Now on KALW, along with his co-hosted podcasts, demands a different set of operational priorities.
